Free legal aid to poor 
†*281. SHRI ABHAY KANT PRASAD: Will the Minister  of LAW AND 
JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the amount proposed to be provided to the poor 
people in the country under the facility of 'Free legal aid to poor';

2 

[22 December, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(b) the number of people in Jharkhand to whom free legal aid has 
been provided during the last four years; 
(c) whether Government propose to increase the limit of legal aid in 
this regard; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE AND COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on 
the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) In terms of sub-sections (c) and (j) of Section 4 of the Legal 
Services Authorities Act, 1987, the National Legal Services Authority 
(NALSA) allocates funds, on financial  year basis, to the State Legal 
Services Authorities, including Supreme Court Legal Services 
Committee and Non-Governmental Organizations for implementation 
of legal aid programmes and schemes propagated by NALSA which 
include provision for free legal assistance to the poor. During the current 
financial year starting from 1st April 2003 to 30th November, 2003, 
funds amounting to Rs. 2,42,80,000/ - have been allocated by NALSA 
so far No fund has been allocated by NALSA to Jharkhand State Legal 
Services Authority during the current financial year 2003-04. However, 
they were permitted by the competent  Authority to carry over of the 
unutilized funds of Rs. 10 lacs allotted during the year 2002-03 to be 
utilized in the current financial year 2003-04. 
(b) State Legal Services Author ity in Jharkhand had started 
functioning from February 2002. The number of persons given free legal 
aid in the state is as under:-  
Financial Year Number of Legal Aid Beneficiaries 
2001-2002 NIL 
2002-03 203 
2003-04 454 
(upto 30.11.2003)  
3 

RAJYA SABHA [22 December, 2003] 
(c) and (d) Under Section 12 of t he Legal Services Authorities Act, 
1987, every person whose annual income does not exceed Rs. 9,000 is 
eligible for free legal aid in cases coming before High Courts and Courts 
subordinate thereto. In cases before the Supreme Court, the limit has 
been Rs. 12,000/-. This limit can be enhanced by the Central/State 
Government, as the case may be. Limitation as to the income does not 
apply in cases of persons belonging to the scheduled castes, scheduled 
tribes, women, children, handicapped etc. At the first annual meet of the 
State Legal Services Authorities held under the aegis of the NALSA on 
12th September, 1998 at New Delhi, it was unanimously resolved that for 
cases before High Courts and Courts subordinate thereto, the minimum 
income ceiling in every State should be raised to Rs. 25,000/- per annum 
and for the cases before the Supreme Court of India, it should be raised 
to Rs. 50,000/- per annum. Accordingly, the Government has enhanced 
the annual income ceiling to Rs. 50,000/- for the cases before the Supreme 
Court. Barring, Arunachal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir, Meghalaya, West 
Bengal, Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Daman & Diu and Lakshadweep, the 
income ceiling limit has since been enhanced. The income ceiling limit in 
Jharkhand is Rs. 25,000/-.

SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the danger of consuming pesticides and 
chemicals with food is high in the country, largely due to inept 
administrative control and lack of will of the authorities to implement the 
laws on food safety; 
(b) whether the recent controversy of pesticide residues in soft drinks, 
insect infestations in chocolates are just some examples of the danger 
that exists; and 
(c) if so, the action taken by Government thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
†The question was actually asked on the floor   of the House   by Shri 
Prem Chand Gupta. 
15 

RAJYA SABHA [22 December, 2003] 
Statement 
The use of pesticides is regulated under the Insecticide Act, 1968, 
which is implemented by the Ministry of Agriculture. Under the Insecticide 
Act, the Registration Committee (RC) registers pesticides for use upon 
specified food crops only after satisfyi ng itself regarding their efficacy, 
residues and safety to human beings, animals and the matters connected 
therewith. 
If the approved/registered pesticides are used on food crops as per 
the recommended doses and as per direction given on the lable and 
leaflets, these are not likely to pose health hazards to human beings and 
animals. 
For safety to human health, maximum residue limits (MRLs) have 
been prescribed for different pesticides for various foods by the Ministry 
of Health under Rule 65 of the PFA Rules, 1955. Keeping in view in 
residues of pesticides in different components including food items, the 
Government of Indis ia advocating Integrated Pest Management (IPM) 
which inter alia includes the need based and judicious use of pesticides, 
use of bio-pesticides, banning/phasing out the most persistent 
organochlorine group of pesticides, educating farmers on judicious use 
of pesticides and observance of waiting period and encouraging the organic 
farming. 
The standard for chocolate has been prescribed under PFA Rules. 
Subsequent to recent media reports regarding insect infestation from 
Maharashtra, instructions have been issued to all regional officers for 
random inspection and sampling to prevent such occurrence. A draft 
notification has been issued for prescribing maximum pesticide residues 
in soft drinks for which public comments have been invited. Meanwhile, 
a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) to look into the issues of 
pesticides in soft drinks etc. has been constituted to suggest criteria for 
evolving suitable safety standard for soft drinks, fruit juice other 
beverages where what is the main constituent.

Outbreak of Mysterious Disease in U.P. 
*285. PROF. M. SANKARAUNGAM: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the fact that a mystery fever 
has killed 20 persons in Saharanpur, Uttar Pradesh; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether similar cases have been reported in any other part of 
the country; and 
(d) if so, the steps taken to contain it? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
Statement 
As per available information, there was an outbreak in Saharanpur 
and other adjoining districts of Mujaffarnagar and Haridwar in Uttar Pradesh 
where children upto the age of 10 years reported symptoms of fever 
and altered sensorium of less than 7 days duration leading, in some 
cases, to coma and death. In all, 109 cases (male 56 and female 53) 
were reported of which 78 died. 
On the request of the State Health  authorities, a team of experts 
was deputed by the Dte. General of Health Services, Government of 
India. The team visited the affected places between 18.10.03 and 
20.10.03. Upon investigation, the diagnosis was of viral encephalitis of 
which 7 have tested positive for Japanese encephalitis. 
Out-breaks with somewhat similar symptoms were also reported in 
Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra in the month of July this year. On the 
request of the State Health authorities, these were investigated by teams 
from the NICD and ICMR. In Maharashtra, the conclusion of the team 
was in favour of encephalitis, probably viral in origin. In Andhra Pradesh, 
the clinical epidemiological and available laboratory evidence pointed 
towards viral encephalitis with a likely possibility of Japanese 
encephalitis. 
26

In the affected areas, for the containment of vector, the State Health 
authorities took up spray with Pyrethrum, malathion fogging and use of 
larvicides. The Central Government provided requisite technical and other 
support. For effecting surveillance of  such out-breaks, a World Bank 
assisted Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) is on the 
anvil. Japanese Encephalitis has been included in the National Vector 
Borne Disease Control Programme which has been approved by the 
Government recently. With this the Central Government will be in a better 
position to assist State Governments in containment of outbreaks due to 
virus transmitted by vectors.

Removal of Non-Tariff Barriers 
*288. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state; 
(a) whether the World Bank authorities have urged upon Government 
to cut tariffs and remove non-tariff barriers with immediate effect; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the context in which the suggestion 
has been made; and 
(c) Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ARUN 
JAITLEY): (a) to (c) In May 2003, the World Bank came out with a 
draft report on "Trade Policies in South Asia: An Overview" in which it 
has taken into account the trade policy reforms being implemented in 
five South Asian countries, namely , India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, 
Bangladesh and Nepal. The report focuses on some key areas of trade 
policy and inter alia recommends lowering of tariffs and removal of non-
tariff barriers. The report has not correctly reflected the facts about India 
in several aspects and these have been communicated to the World 
Bank authorities. 
46 

[22 December, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
In another World Bank report "India-Sustaining Reform, Reducing 
Poverty" published in July 2003, following the Bank's review of the 
country's development policies, some suggestions have been made 
regarding reduction of India's import tariffs over the next three to four 
years and to reduce its World Trade Organization (WTO) agricultural tariff 
bindings to much lower levels. The views contained in the report are that 
of the World Bank and do not reflect as such the views of the Government. 
However, Indian import tariffs are well below the WTO bound rates and 
reduction of peak rates of customs duties and duly rate rationalization 
has been an integral part of India's economic reforms.

Effects of Adulterated Food on Health 
*292. SHRI AMAR SINGH: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that unbridled use of pesticides and chemicals 
in the production of food items causes genetic or bio-chemical disorder; 
(b) if so, whether it is also a fact that Government have neither 
prescribed any Food Safety Code nor decided to implement sincerely the 
existing food laws like Fruit Products Order, Milk and Milk Product Order, 
Vegetable Oil Control Order despite the press reports regarding pesticides 
residues in soft drinks and mineral water and insect infection in chocolates 
etc.; and 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor and by when the remedial measures 
are proposed to be taken? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) to (c) The use of registered pesticides 
within prescribed limits as per approved guidelines is not likely to cause 
any genetic or biochemical disorder either in food or in human beings. At 
the time of registration, besides chemistry, bioefficacy, packaging, toxicity 
data on acute oral, acute dermal, acute inhalation, mutagenicity, 
teratogenicity, effect on reproducti on, carcinogenicity, toxicity to 
livestock and Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI) are also taken into 
consideration. 
The regulatory orders like, Fruit Products Order, Milk & Milk 
Products Order, Vegetable Oil Product (Regulation) Order, 1998, have 
been enacted under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955, which 
primarily regulate licensing and hygi ene besides quality specifications 
and are being Implemented by the respective Departments of the 
Government of India. 
49 

RAJYA SABHA [22 December, 2003] 
The Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and PFA Rule, 1955, 
prescribes the standards for various foods besides regulating use of food 
additives, limits food contaminants, an d pesticides etc. The role of the 
central Government is to facilitate the State Governments in implementing 
the provisions of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and PFA 
Rule, 1955. The actual licensing of manufacturing units and enforcement 
of the standards under the law is the function of the State Governments. 
For safety to human Health, maximum residue limits (MRLs) have been 
prescribed for different pesticides for various foods by Ministry of Health 
under Rule 65 of the PFA Rules, 1955.  Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare has prescribed MRLs for 71 pesticides and maximum residues 
limits for another 50 pesticides hav e been notified for soliciting public 
comments. 
Under the Capacity Building Proj ect launched by the Central 
Government in October, 2003, support is being provided to the State 
Governments for strengthening their food laboratories and also for 
setting up of new food laboratories wherever required. The Prevention of 
Food Adulteration Act, 1954, is also being reviewed in order to ensure 
consumer safety.

Cancer Vaccine 
*296. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister 
of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a multi use vaccine to fight different forms of cancer is 
likely to hit the market shortly; and 
(b) if so, the name of the vaccine, its price and the types of cancer to 
be treated by this vaccine? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) and (b) According to the Indian 
Council of Medical Research (ICMR), at present there are two approaches 
for development of cancer vaccines-(i) preventive (ii) immuno-therapeutic. 
Vaccines such as Heptitis 'B' viru s and Human Papiloma Virus (HPV) 
vaccine which may prevent the infectio ns that may cause liver cancer 
and cervical cancer respectively can be classified as preventive in nature. 
The immuno-therapeutic cancer vaccine may enhance the immunity in 
cancer patient and help in containing the disease. The Hepatitis 'B' vaccine 
is already available in the Indian market and HPV vaccine is undergoing 
clincial trails in. USA and other countries. Clinical trial of this vaccine is 
also likely to be undertaken in India. The immuno-therapeutic vaccines 
being developed in USA and other countries are in the developing stages 
and are required to undergo regulatory mechanisms preceding they could 
be put to human use. Further, such cancern vaccines developed by other 
countries are required to follow the regulatory mechanism of Drug 
Controller General of India {DCG(I)} before they could be used for cancer 
management in the country. There are no multi-use vaccines to fight 
different forms of cancer, which are likely to come in the market in India 
shortly.

Health care to poor children 
*300. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that proj ect study conducted by the Institute 
of Development Studies, supported by a British Organisation "Save the 
Children" in two districts of Banswara and Tonk to explore how childhood 
poverty varies between chronic and transient areas has revealed that 
health issues of children have always been ignored in the mainstream 
development policies; 
(b) if so, what corrective measures have been taken to ensure that

60  

[22 December, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) and (b) No, Sir. The study is called 
CHIP (Childhood Poverty) in Rajasthan. This is an ongoing research project 
funded by DFID (Department for International Development), London. 
The CHIP Research and Policy Centre is a Collaborative venture between 
SC (Save the Children) UK (United Kingdom) and CPRC (Chronic Poverty 
Research Centre) led by Manchester University. The research study is 
taking place in four countries, India being one. In India, the study is led 
by IDS (Institute of Development Studies, Jaipur) and is conducted in 
four villages (two in Banswara and two in Tonk district) of Rajasthan. SC 
UK in India is overseeing the research work but the main coordination is 
done by SC CHIP Team based in London. 
The objective of the study is to measure the factors that shape childhood 
poverty and gather evidence of inter generational transfer of poverty, factors 
that break poverty cycles and policies and strategies that are in place 
address childhood poverty. The study was commissioned in April 2002 
and after the initial planning, the actual research work started from January 
2003. The field research is still continuing and we hope to have the 
preliminary report by end of April, 2004. 
An advisory committee has been set up that provides guidance and 
advice to the research work. The Advisory Committee have members 
that include representative from DWCD (Department of Women and Child), 
Rajasthan, UNICEF, Rajasthan and IIPA (Indian Institute of Public 
Administration), Delhi. 
(c) Study on all-India basis would depend upon result of study called 
CHIP.

and/or coloring, India has stated that they should be used to distinguish

feasible and does not have a significant impact on price. The developing 
countires wanted to arrive at a decision which would enable manufacture 
and export of pharmaceutical product s under compulsory license to 
countires with limited or no manufacturing capacity in the pharmaceutical 
sector. The Decision would provide an opportunity to generic companeis

Infection Control Programme 
2036. SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the latest position with regard to the programme for improvement 
of infection control and waste management through appropriate methods; 
and 
(b) whether any significant progress has been noticed by Government? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) to (b) The Government of India 
(Ministry of Environment & Forests) has notified Bio-Medical Waste 
(Management & Handling) Rules, 1998 under Environment (Protection) 
Act, 1986. These Rules have prescribed mandatory steps to ensure 
handling of Bio-Medical waste without any adverse effect to human health 
and environment. This Ministry also has a programme under which financial 
assistance to the tune of Rs. 1.50 crores is provided to the State 
Government Hospitals for upgradation/creation of infrastructure for 
management of bio-medical waste. 
In so far as Central Government Hospitals are concerned, an Infection 
Control Committee is in existence in each of the hospital and the Hospital 
Waste is disposed of as per the guidelines laid under the Bio-Medical 
Waste (Management & Handling) Rules, 1998. All these efforts have led 
to an improvement in management and control of infection in the hospitals.

Health project to improve life

2039. MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have launched a health project to improve 
the life span of women and bring down the high rate of infant mortality in 
Orissa; if so, the details of the project; 
(b) whether under this project it is also proposed to improve literacy 
rate among women; and 
(c) the progress achieved in its implementation till date? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) The reproductive and Child Health 
(RCH) Programme, which aims at bringing down infant and maternal 
mortality and improving the health status of young children and pregnant 
women, has been under implementation since Oct., 1997 in all States of 
the country including Orissa. The interventions which focus on bringing 
down infant mortality include immunization against six vaccine 
preventable disease, essential new born care, control of deaths due to 
diarrhoea and pneumonia, prophylaxis of Vitamin-A deficiency and 
promotion of exclusive breast feeding. The interventions focused on 
pregnant women include, essential obstetric care promotion of institutional 
and safe deliveries, provision of em ergency obstetric care and referral 
transportation for women, from in degent families requiring emergency 
care. 
100 

[22 December, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
The Government of Orissa have launched infant mortality reduction 
mission w.e.f. 15.8.2001 to accelerate the decline of infant mortality from 
97/1000 live births to 60/1000 live birt hs by 2005. Under the mission, 
steps have been initiated by Government of Orissa to improve antenatal 
care services including protection of pregnant women against malaria, 
improve institutional and safe deliveries, new born care, ensure complete 
immunization, ensure early detection of cases of pneumonia, diarrhoea, 
malnutrition, measles and providing referral and basic curative services 
by strengthening the health services. 
(b) Improving literacy rate, as such, is not a component of the 
programme. However, awareness and education of women and families 
on health issues is undertaken through the Information, Education & 
Communication (IEC) component of the RCH Programme. 
(c) The IMR of Orissa has shown a decline from 97/1000 live birth 
in 2001 to 87/1000 live birth in 2002.

2045. DR. ALLADI P. RAJKUMAR: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that 'persuasive' methods have failed to 
check population in the country during the past 55 years; and 
(b) if so, the steps proposed/plann ed to control population in view 
of gravity of the problem? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) and (b) The trend of population growth 
104 

[22 December, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
in India is fairly in tune with the classical theory of demographic transition. 
The country has passed through all the successive phases of demographic 
transition and is now widely believed to have entered in a phase that is 
usually characterized by rapidly dec lining fertility: The average annual 
exponential growth rate of population increased from 1.25% in 1951 to 
2.22% in 1981, after which it has declined to 2.14% in 1991 and further 
dipped to 1.93% in 2001. 
The Government has adopted the Target Free Approach since 1996 
and the Family Welfare Programme in India is voluntary in nature. The 
Government aims at improvement in access to quality Maternal and

Eradication of TB, Malaria and Leprosy 
2082. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether inspite of Government schemes for complete eradication 
of malaria, leprosy and tuberculosis such patients are increasing day by 
day; 
146 

[22 December, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(b) whether thousands of people are dying of Malaria, brain malaria, 
SARS, dengue not only in rural areas but also in metropolitan cities 
including Delhi; and 
(c) whether Government have any action plan for eradication of 
malaria, TB and leprosy? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) to (c) The reported cases of malaria have been 
recording a declining trend since 1996. 3.03 million ca ses of malaria 
were reported in 1996 as compared to 1.99 million cases in 2002. 1.00 
million cases have been reported during this year up to 25th November, 
2003. 
The Number of deaths due to malaria and dengue in the country 
as well as metro cities inlcudng Delhi in 2003 as per reports received 
from States upto 25th November, 2003 are as under:  
Area Malaria Dengue 
Country total 577 209 
Delhi 0 34 
Kolkata 11 0 
Chennai 0 2 
Mumbai 5 10 
Early diagnosis and prompt treatment and integrated vector control 
are the strategies adopted by the Government to control malaria. The 
programme is implemented by the State Health Authorities while material 
and technical support are provided by Government of India. There is an 
appreciable decline in the number of cases of leprosy in the country. The 
prevalence rate of leprosy at national level has come down from 57.6 
cases per 10,000 in March 1981 to 3.2 per 10,000 population on 1st 
April, 2003. The estimated number of leprosy cases was 4 million in 
1981 whereas the recorded cases as on 1st April, 2003 was only 3.4 
lakhs. 
For elimination of leprosy the Govt. of India is implementing the 
2nd World Bank assisted National Leprosy Elimination Project for the 
period 2001-2004. 
147 

RAJYA SABHA [22 December, 2003] 
The National Leprosy Eradication Programme is being implemented 
as a 100% centrally sponsored scheme in all the States/UTs of the country 
with the objective of reaching the level of elimination i.e. leprosy cases 
less than one per ten thousand population in the country by 2005. 
The number of TB cases being repo rted over the last few years 
under the National TB Control Programme have been more or less static. 
Due to epidemiological situation pertaining to TB, it is technically not 
possible to eradicat the disease at this point of time. Government of 
India is operating the National TB Control Programme (NTCP) to control 
the disease. 
For the control of TB, in order to achieve a cure rate of 85% of new 
sputum positive cases and to detect at least 70% of such cases, Revised 
National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) is being implemented in the 
country in a phased manner. About 770 million population have been 
covered in about 425 districts of the country. It is envisaged to cover 850 
million population by 2004 and the entire country by 2005. (85%). Currently 
8 out of every 10 patients treated for TB are being completely-cured. 
Only three cases of SARS were repored in India, all imported from 
affected countries. The action taken by  Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare in coordination with the State Government had prevented outbreak 
of SARS in the country.

Recommendations of Delhi High Court 
2117. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the recommendations made 
by Delhi High Court that "Respons ibility of court administration should 
be left to the judiciary and that the Government should have no control 
over it" and "That judiciary is blamed for all the failures in the 
administration of justice whereas c ontrol over appointment of judges 
and financial component of the justice delivery mechanism, remains with 
Government"; and 
(b) if so, the Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LAW AND 
JUSTICE (SHRI P.C. THOMAS): (a) and (b) The Delhi High Court in its 
judgment in a Criminal Case, CrI. M(M) No. 2686/2003 observed that the 
Government should transfer the responsibility of court administration 
179 

RAJYA SABHA [22 December, 2003] 
exclusively to the judiciary as ultimately the public blames the judiciary 
for all ills and failures of administration of justice though the entire control 
about availability of judges, supply of administrative component and 
financial sanction vests in the Government. 
The above observation arose out of an appeal filed by a private party 
for summary disposal of a cheque bouncing case under Section 138 of 
Negotiable Instrument Act. 
Articles 233, 234 and 235 of the Constitution provide ample power 
to the High Court of the concerned State in matters of administration of 
subordinate courts such as appointment  of district judges, recruitment 
of persons other than district judges,  the control over district courts 
and courts subordinate to it incl uding posting and promotion and the 
grant of leave to persons belonging to the judicial service. 
In view of the above, no action was considered necessary on the 
observation of the Delhi High Court and it was noted for future reference 
only.

Housing Scheme for Urban poor 
2147. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the housing schemes formulated by Government 
for poor people in the urban areas of the country; and 
(b) the financial assistance likely to be provided by Government, 
scheme-wise during the Tenth Plan? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) Housing is a Stat e subject. Government of India 
acts only as a facilitator and not as a provider. However, Housing & 
Urban Development Corporation Lt d. (HUDCO), a public sector 
enterprise under this Ministry, provides housing finance to various 
State agencies for housing schemes including those for the weaker 
sections of the society. HUDCO provides housing finance based on 
demand driven approach. It is for State agecies to submit projects 
proposals for the assistace from HUDCO, according to their 
requirements. 
In order to facilitate construction of adequate housing facilities 
particularly for Economically Weaker Sections and Low Income Group, 
Government has launched the Two Million Housing Programme under 
which 7 lakh houses will be constructed in Urban areas every year. This 
programme is implemented through Housing & Urban Development 
Corporation Ltd. (HUDCO), Housing finance Institutions, Public Sector 
Banks and Cooperative Sector. 
Government has also launched a Centrally sponsored Scheme 
named Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana (VAMBAY) on 2.12.2001, with 
the aim to provide shelter or upgrade the existing shelter for the people 
living below poverty line including members of Economically Weaker 
Sections who do not posses adequate shelter in urban slums and 
enabling urban environment through construction of community toilets 
226 

[22 December, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
under Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan, a component of VAMBAY. This scheme is 
shared between Centre and State in the ratio of 50:50. 
(b)TheTwo Million Housing Programme is a demand driven scheme. 
No financial allocation is earmarked in the budget for this scheme during 
the Tenth Plan as it is essentially a loan based scheme. HUDCO and 
other organisations have been extending loans to Housing Boards and 
other parastatals against projects for implementing the programme. In 
2002-03 viz. First Year of the Tenth Plan, the Urban Housing sanctions 
have been as follows:— 
HUDCO Rs. 2792.91 crore 
Cooperative Sector Rs. 1287.09 crore 
HFIs/Banks Rs. 19148.71 crore 
A similar amount is estimated to be spent annually towards urban 
housing during the remaining years of the Tenth Plan. The total outlay 
for VAMBAY in the Tenth Plan is Rs. 2040 crore.

Wastage of Drinking Water 
2155. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that 40 per cent of drinking 
water in NCT of Delhi is wasted every year and the local agencies are 
unable to take any remedial steps; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
237 

RAJYA SABHA [22 December, 2003] 
(c) whether Government are losing a lot of revenue on account of 
wasted of water; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof during the last two years? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA) (a) and (b) The Delhi Jal Board (DJB) has reported 
that it is not correct that 40 percent of drinking water in NCT of Delhi is 
wasted every year. As a matter of fact the figure includes free water 
supply, tanker water supply to weaker sections, lines losses and theft. 
To improve the position, the DJB has taken remedial measures 
like replacement of about 1100 Kms. of old corroded water lines to 
minimize losses to leakages, setting up of a separate Leak Detection 
Investigation Cell for plugging leakages. DJB maintains a fleet of about 
1000 water tankers for free supply of  water to deficient areas which 
constitute substantial percentage of total non-revenue water. 
(c) and (d) Some wastage of water to distribution system and lines 
losses are inherent in the system s involving vast water pipeline 
networks. However, no bench marking has been done in the country 
to establish the quantum of losses on this account. As per the policy of 
Delhi Jal Board and the Government of NCT of Delhi water supply to 
weaker sections and deficient areas through tankers/public hydrants is 
made free of cost and cannot be termed as financial losses.

Urban slums in Bihar 
†2158. SHRIMATI KUM KUM RAI: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the fact that the number of 
slums has increased manifold in the urban area of Bihar during the 
last decade; 
(b) if so, whether Government has conducted any survey in this 
regard; 
(c) if so, the outcome thereof; 
(d) the steps proposed to be ta ken by Government to prevent 
increasing trend of slums in the State; and 
(e) the steps Government propose to  take to provide amenities in 
slums of the State with the assistance of the State Government? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) to (c) Slum Development being a State subject, 
State Governments survey and take st ock of slums in their respective 
States. However, the Town and Country Planning Organisation (TCPO) 
conducted a one time study on slums in 1995-96 and brought out a 
report titled "a Compendium on Indian Slums-1996". According to this 
report, the estimated slum population of Bihar (including Jharkhand) in 
1991 was 26.9 lakh and estimated to be 35.44 lakhs in 2001. 
An attempt was made for the first time during the Census of India, 
2001 by the Registrar General of I ndia to collect detailed data about 
slum population of the country but only in cities/towns having 50,000 
population or more based on 1991 Census. As per the provisional 
figures of Census of India, the total provisional slum population of 
Bihar is 5.07 lakh. 
(d) and (e) With a view to ameliorate the living conditions of the slum 
dwellers a programme known as National Slum Development Programme 
(NSDP) was launched at the National level by the Government in August, 
1996 for the development of urban slums, Funds under NSDP are 
allocated as Additional Central Assi stance (ACA) to various States on 
the basis of pro-rata slum population.

2161. SHRI RAMA SHANKER KAUSHIK: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that th e Central Government Employees' 
Welfare Housing Organisation (CGEWHO) facilitates formation of the 
Resident's Welfare Association while handing over possession of Flats 
in the Projects constructed by it in its various Housing Schemes; 
(b) if so, the details of the procedure adopted by it for formation of 
such associations; 
(c) whether such an association would also be formed in NOIDA 
Phase-Ill Housing Scheme; and 
(d) if so, what amount would be provided by the CGEWHO to the 
Association? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The procedure adopted is in Para 31 
of Part B-CGEWHO Rules gove rning NOIDA Housing Schemes— 
Phase-Ill Statement (See below). 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. 1. 5% of the cost of flats in charged from the 
beneficiaries towards Apartment Owners' Association (AOA) charges 
and credited to the Apartment Owners' Association/Society, as and when 
formed as per the above rules (Statement). 
Statement 
Extract from CGEWHO rules NOIDA Housing Scheme—Phase-Ill  
(Part-B)para 31. Cooperative Society/Apartment Owners' 
Association 
Beneficiaries of each Scheme woul d form a Cooperative Society/ 
Apartment Ownership Association under local laws governing such bodies. 
Every beneficiary will pay the Membership Fee for the Society/association. 
In addition, a sum equal to 1.5% of the final cost of the dwelling unit will 
be charged from each beneficiary and credited to the account of his 
245 

RAJYA SABHA [22 December, 2003] 
Society/Association, for its running expenses. The Society/Association, 
will administer the colony, look after it maintenance, attend to common 
property and provide guidelines fo r civic standards. The Society/ 
Association will be governed by its bye-laws. 
Procedure & Obligations: 
(a) Coinciding with or after completion of the project, CGEWHO will 
hold a General Body meeting of all the beneficiaries to elect the office-
bearers of the proposed Apartment Owners' Association. 
(b) Such elected ad-hoc committee, of the proposed Apartment 
Owners' Association, will aim at formally constituting the Association, 
including framing of its by-laws under the local laws governing such bodies, 
and register the same with the appropriate competent authorities. 
(c) On completing the formalities regarding registration of the 
Association, the ad-hoc Committee would be required to convene a 
General Body meeting of all the beneficiaries to elect and constitute a 
regular Managing/Executive Committee. 
(d)The duly elected ad-hocCommittee will take over all the common 
areas/services/facilities of the project within 6 months of its constitution— 
a period during which CGEWHO will ma intain the residential complex 
and debit the actual maintenance expenses so incurred to the Apartment 
Owners' Association account. 
(e) In case the ad-hoclrequ\ax Committee fails to take over the 
common services/facilities areas with in a further period of 4 months, the 
CGEWHO shall be at liberty to wind up its operations at site, including 
demobilising its manpower, leaving the complex in 'as is-where is' 
condition, at the discretion of t he Chief Executive Officer, CGEWHO. 
However, during these 4 months period, though the CGEWHO shall 
maintain the complex at the cost of Apartment Owners' Association, it 
will charge an additional amount of Rs. 100/ per beneficiary per month for 
the services so provided which will be over and above the actual cost of 
maintenance and debit the same to the Apartment Owner's Association 
account, before handing over the balance of amount to it.

Poverty alleviation programmes for slum dwellers 
2162. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are implementing the poverty alleviation 
programmes for the slum dwellers and urban poor; and 
(b) whether Government have any scheme to cover the parents of all 
the identified child labour under these programmes? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF  THE MINISTRY OR URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) The Ministry of Urban Development & Poverty 
Alleviation has been implementing Swarana Jayanti Shahari Rojgar Yojana 
(SJSRY), a Centrally sponsored urban poverty alleviation scheme, with 
effect from 1.12.1997 subsuming all previous programmes, for the benefit 
of urban poor, on all India basis, with a view to providing gainful 
employment to the urban unemployed or under-employed poor through, 
firstly, encouraging the setting up of self-employment ventures by those, 
who have studied upto 9th standard and  secondly, by providing wage 
employment by utilising their labour  for construction of socially and 
economically useful public assets. The scheme is funded in the ratio of 
75:25 between the Centre and the States. 
(b) There is no such Urban Poverty Alleviation Scheme to cover the 
parents of all the identified child labour.

month of January 
SHRI A. VIJAYA RAGHAVAN (KERALA): Madam, it is very 
unfortunate that the Christmas holidays of Kendriya Vidyalayas has been 
deferred to January. In Kendriya Vidyalayas, usually the holidays begin

examinations. Madam, ours is a pluralistic society. We have always given

be maintained. Thank you, Madam.

DR. MANMOHAN SINGH (Assam): Madam, the Appropriation Bill 
provides an opportunity for us to take stock of the developments in the 
economy during the current financial year, and this task has been 
facilitated by the Government's own Mid Year Review which has been 
brought out a few weeks ago. There is, today, a lot of advertisement 
blitz about shining India. We all would like our country to shine brighter 
and brighter, but this cannot come  about unless we have a coherent 
strategy to deal with those constraints which, hitherto, have held us back 
and have prevented us from utilising or realising the immense 
development potential that our country, undoubtedly, has. The Mid year 
Review notes that as a result of a favourable monsoon this year, the 
agricultural output will probably, increase by eight per cent, and that, 
with industry growing at six per cent, services growing at over seven per 
cent, the economy should register a growth rate of over seven per cent. 
It is, indeed, fortunate that this year's monsoon has been good, that the 
growth rate of economy has gone up. But this improvement in the growth 
rate has to be reviewed against the background of an abysmal growth 
performance of the economy last year, when the growth was no more 
than 4.3 per cent. 
(MR. CHAIRMAN in the Chair) 
And if I look at the last five y ears, since this Government has been 
in office, the average growth rate of the economy does not exceed 5 to 
5.5 per cent. We are, today, in the second year of the Tenth Five Year 
Plan, and if the Government's own figures are to be believed, then, the 
growth rate of the economy in the first two years of the Plan will also not 
exceed 5.5 per cent. Therefore, one would have expected, from the Mid-
Year Review, an assessment of our ability of achieve the eight per cent 
growth target, which is the target laid down in the Eighth Five Year Plan. 
As I see it, current trend does not create sufficient confidence that the 
economy, in fact, is on a growth path of eight per cent. 
273 

RAJYA SABHA [22 December, 2003] 
We ail know that there are today a number of favourable 
circumstances in the economy. For a long period, food and foreign 
exchange were dominant constraint on the development of our economy. 
Fortunately, both these constraints are a thing of the past and yet we 
find that economy has got stuck to a growth path of not more than 5.5 
per cent. We need an in-depth analysis of why this is so. The Review, 
unfortunately, does not enlighten us on this crucial point. In fact, when I 
look at the underpinning of growth, investments rate and saving rate, I 
find that the peak rates were reached in 1995-96. Both in terms of 
aggregate investments and in terms of gross domestic savings, the peak 
was reached in 1995-96. Since then the economy has been hovering at 
lower rates of investment and lower rates of savings. 
In fact, both capital formation in the private corporate sector and 
capital formation in the public sector have been much lower in recent 
years that what it was in the mid nineties, particularly, in the year 1995-
96. Therefore, one would like to know  what is it that will change the 
situation from 5.5 per cent to 8 per cent growth rate. The Ninth Plan had 
an average savings rate of 23.3 percent. The terminal year of the Plan 
had a savings rates of about 24 per cent and the Tenth Plan has a savings 
rate average of 26.8 per cent; the terminal year's average would be 
about 29.4 per cent. We are nowhere in sight of reaching these savings 
rates. If these savings rates are no t realised, our ability to achieve a 
growth rate of 8 per cent and to finance it in a non-inflationary method 
would be seriously in doubt. 
In fact, Sir, the situation with regard to public sector savings has 
shown a sharp deterioration in the last five or six years. In 1995-96, the 
public sector savings rate was about 2 per cent of the GDP. In recent 
years, the public sector savings, both Central and States combined, 
have been a negative figure of 2.5 per cent of GDP; therefore, there is a 
deterioration of 4.5 per cent of the GDP. If the Government had a strategy 
to deal with this negative turn in the public sector savings rate, the 
country's public finances would have improved greatly and the problems 
of fiscal deficit and revenue deficit, which bedevil us, would have been,

[22 December, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
I think, more amenable to viable practical solutions. Unfortunately, I don't 
find any analysis of the public sector savings, the behaviour, the current 
trend and the prospects, as far as the Review is concerned. In the 
same way, I have mentioned that as far as gross domestic capital 
formation, that is, investment, is concerned, both in the private corporate 
sector and in the public sector, the rates of investment, in fact, have 
been much lower in recent years that what they were in the mid nineties. 
Therefore, I would like to ask the hon. Finance Minister to enlighten the 
House as to how, in the light of current trends of savings and investments 
and growth rate of the economy, does he visualise the prospect of our 
achieving a growth rate of 8 per cent in the Tenth Five year Plan. 
In fact, Sir, if I look at the growth  rate during the current year, it is 
certainly true that agriculture is going to do better. That is an act of 
God. Fortunately, weather Gods hav e been favourable. But even then 
the agriculture growth rate in the last five years shows a sharp decline. 
The trend rate of agricultural growth in our country long-term trend, is 
about 3 per cent. In the last five years, we have been, in fact, moving at 
a lower trend rate. If we look at the fluctuations in the last five years, 
fluctuations in agricultural output have also increased very sharply. Sir, 
we all want that agriculture should do better. But, for that, we need a lot 
more investment in irrigation; we need a lot more investment in agricultural 
research and extension; we need a lot more attention to rural electrification; 
we need a lot more investments in rural connectivity. All these are areas 
which happen to be in the domain of State Governments. And, the State 
finances being what they are, I do not have the confidence that the States 
are going to invest to the extent that they ought to be investing in irrigation, 
in rural electrification, in refrigeration and in rural connectivity. If, therefore, 
there has to be a better future for our agriculture, the State finances have 
to improve much more sharply than is the case right now. 
With regard to industrial production, the Mid-Year Review projects a 
growth rate of six per cent during the current financial year. The same 
growth rate as recorded last year. Last year, of course, was a drought 
year. But industrial growth rate of 6 percent in the current year cannot be 
considered satisfactory. If this is all that we are aiming at, despite a

favourable monsoon, despite a sharp improvement in India's balance of 
payments, despite large stocks of f oodgrains, then, there is something 
wrong with regard to the formulation of the macro-economic policy. As I 
said earlier food and foreign exchange are no longer the dominant 
constraints, on our development. Then, why is it that we are struck at the 
Industrial growth rate of no more than six per cent? Obviously, adequate 
investment is not taking place. It is not taking place in the public sector;

think, the picture, in fact this year, is only marginally better than the

September, 02, the growth rate of infrastructure—six industries included

4.2 per cent in April-September, 03. 
Sir we all want electricity sector to do much better. But the generation 
of electricity has been dismal in t he last three years. In the year 2000-
2001, the electricity generation in our country increased by no more 
than 3.9 per cent; in the year 2001-02. The growth rate declined to 3.1

refinery where there is a marginal increase from 5.6 per cent to 6.1 per

SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN (Mahar ashtra): Thank you, Madam 
Chairperson. Counterfeit stamp paper scandal, which has rocked the 
country, is unprecedented in the history of this country to say the least. 
The extent of revenue loss, although this revenue was due only to the 
State Governments, is mind-boggling. 
(SHRI RAMA SHANKER KAUSHIK in the Chair) 
And, even today, Government has not come forward with the exact 
extent of the revenue lost by ail the State Governments taken together 
335 

RAJYA SABHA [22 December, 2003] 
ever since the counterfeit printing operations began. Very responsible 
functionaries of the Central Govern ment have themselves contributed 
to the confusion by alluding to the very big numbers. And, I think, as a 
result of this discussion, the co untry will be grateful if the Union 
Finance Minister officially puts to rest the speculation about the extent 
of damage, what it could have do ne to the finances of the State 
Government and also where has this money gone. Sir, very responsible 
journals have quoted figures of something like Rs. 32,000 crores, Rs. 
39,000 crores. The lawyer representing this Mr. Telgi has even gone 
higher. And, even now, no official figure, a State-wise break-up of who 
could have lost what kind of revenu e, has come from the Government. 
It is a difficult task, but not an impossible one. It should not be difficult 
for the Government to reconcile as to what was the total amount of 
transaction entered into the Registrar's Office in each State, the total 
amount of stamp papers and stamps officially sold through the 
treasuries, shipments made by the India Security Press. All these 
numbers are available and with a little bit of estimation, one could get 
at this figure. And, let us put to rest at once, at one time, all these wild 
allegations and wild speculation as to what is the extent of this scam. 
Sir, I would like to divide this whole scandal into two broad categories. 
One is what happened in the States wherever this scam broke out. We 
hear that there are major developments in nine States, papers were 
sold in 17 States, and 77 or 80 cities, but the main operations were 
focussed on two States—Maharashtra and Karnataka—because the 
operations of printing took place in Maharashtra and the man, Mr. 
Telgi, belonged to Karnataka. He was apprehended, arrested many 
times; let off. He was given a royal treatment by police officers and all 
that is one aspect of the case; involvement of police officials and 
involvement of maybe higher-ups. T hat is being enquired into by the 
two Special Investigative Teams cons tituted by the State Government 
of Karnataka and the State Government of Maharashtra. 
Maharashtra's SIT is working under the direction of the Bombay High 
Court, not under the State Government as a result of a Public Interest 
Litigation filed by the social activist, Shri Anna Saheb Hazare, and 
other NGOs. And everybody, including the High Court, which is 
directing this investigation under the leadership of a retired police 
officer, everybody is happy about the way the SIT is investigating this 
case. The Karnataka SIT also has made major

closer towards finishing the investigation, filing charge-sheets and 
prosecution will be launched soon. That is one aspect. 
But, there is the second aspect which deals with the entire machinery 
of printing security documents, whet her it is currency notes, security 
stamps, postage stamps which is the sole responsibility of the Central 
Government, the Ministry of Finance, an d, it is the Ministry of Finance 
which supervises the operations of India Security Press, Nashik or 
Hyderabad, or even the paper mills which are at Hoshangabad, Dewas, 
and, the mints that operate in the country. 
The duplicate or the counterfeit stamp racket would not have taken

been sent out of the premises in good working conditions alongwith 
working printing dyes which were used to print the actual stamp papers

material, equipment was allowed to go out of the premises of India

scrap. There was complete collusion at the highest level between the 
culprit, Telgi and his associates, and, people working and supervising

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
The Fifth Ministerial Conference of WTO held at 
Cancun, Mexico 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE AND MINISTER OF 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): Madam, I beg to make 
a statement before this hon. House regarding the 5th Ministerial Conference of the 
WTO held at Cancun, Mexico during 10—14 September, 2003. 
The Cancun Ministerial Conference was due to take stock of the 
progress in negotiations under the Work Programme launched by the Doha 
Declaration and to provide guidance to negotiators on key areas such as 
agriculture, tariff negotiations for non-agricultural products, special and 
differential treatment and implementation issues. The Conference also had 
to decide on whether or not to launch negotiations on Singapore issues 
based on modalities agred to by 'explicit consensus'. 
In preparation for the Conference, the Government held wide ranging 
consultations with all major stake holders and had accordingly formulated its 
negotiating strategy. This strategy was based on an appreciation of our trade 
interests, development concerns and gains to be made by improving the 
multilateral trading system. We went to Cancun in a positive frame of mind 
with a desire to engage proactively in the negotiations for a fruitful 
outcome. 
The Conference which concluded in Cancun on 14th September, 2003 
could not reach a decision covering all areas. An important reason for the 
lack of a decision at Cancun was the inability of the proposals on the table to 
forge a consensus by taking into account the concerns of all Members on 
many contentious issues. The Conference ended with a Ministerial Statement 
which recognized that more work needed to be done in key areas to enable 
WTO Member countries to proceed towards the conclusion of negotiations under 
the Doha mandate. 
The developments at Cancun have been a disappointment for us. We are 
interested in having a healthy, effective multilateral trading system which would 
provide the institutional backdrop for a process of economic development that 
would benefit all countries. The overriding priority and 
384 
 

 
[22 December, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
consideration for a developing country like India in any trading arrangement 
is the implication of such an arrangement for its economic development. 
This focus on development determines our position on any trade rules 
and proposals at the WTO. Our goal at Cancun on major issues was 
guided by national interest. 
In agriculture, our desire was to ensure that agriculture markets across 
the world are freed from the substantia l distortions that are caused by 
large scale subsidisation. These di stortions prevent agriculture from 
fulfilling its potential of being an engine of growth. Income inequalities 
caused so far by such distortions continue. It is essential in the interests 
of equity, justice and fair play that the distortions in agriculture are 
gradually eliminated. Therefore, agricultural market access in developing 
countries has to be sequenced appropriately with reductions in market 
distortions elsewhere. At the same time, we wish to protect the interest 
of the millions of subsistence level farmers who depend on agriculture as 
their sole means of sustenance. Therefore, there has to be a calibrated 
approach to market access vis-a-vis reduction in distortions in agriculture 
with a transition period in which affected farmers are shielded through 
the use of special safeguard mechanisms and protection for special 
products. In view of all this, expecting us to make onerous market access 
commitments inconsistent with the reality in agriculture was unreasonable. 
The draft modalities on agriculture proposed at Cancun, on the other 
hand, did not take into account these concerns fully and would in all 
probability, have perpetuated distortions. We had no choice but to oppose 
these modalities. 
On tariff negotiations in non-agricultural products, significant 
convergence in negotiating position s could be realized by taking on 
board the concerns of all Members. 
On Singapore Issues, one has to address the question of multilateral 
rule making taking primacy over economic development goals, particularly 
in areas where the interplay between these new issues and development 
is unknown. The Ministerial Conference had to take a decision on 
modalities for all the Singapore Issues. However, this was to be by explicit 
consensus. Discussions clearly revealed that not only was this consensus 
absent but that most developing countries felt that the clarification process 
on these issues had not run its full course. In the absence of clarity on 
many elements, a majority of the membership for the WTO had rejected 
385 

RAJYA SABHA [22 December, 20031 
launch of negotiations on these issues and sought a continuation of the 
clarification process. There were concerns that a framework on Investment would 
constrain the policy space for developing countries in utilizing FDI for their 
developmkent goals. There was no certainty that such a framework would 
lead to larger FDI flows nor was any need for a framework demonstrated. On 
Competition Policy, the issue of encroaching upon the freedom of competition 
authorities was disquieting. The benefits of a framework on Transparency in 
Government Procurement were also not clear. In spite of this, proposals tabled 
suggested launch of negotiations in some areas. In the absence of explicit 
consensus, launching negotiations was however, an impossibility. 
India was disappointed that no time frame was prescribed for resolving 
outstanding implementation issues. These issues highlight the imbalances arising 
out of the Uruguay round agreement and need to be addressed on a priority basis 
so that imbalances brought in by the Uruguay round are redressed. On Special 
and Differential Treatment Issues, India felt that adequate urgency was not 
being shown in addressing these issues. 
An important outcome from our viewpoint is the engagement of 
developing countries in the negotiating process. Unlike in the past, when they 
were blamed for non-participation, the degree of participation of the large group 
of developing countries is a welcome development. Not only having developing 
countries become participants in the process but have also shown adequate 
flexibility to reach out to other fellow countries to form alliances which have been 
formed during and after the conference. The G-20 on Agriculture and the G-16 
on Singapore Issues embody the desire of developing countries to generate 
common positions on issues. 
The Ministerial Conference concluded with a Ministerial Statement which 
recognised that more work needed to be done in some key areas to 
enable WTO Member countries to proceed towards the conclusion of 
negotiations under the Doha mandate. The Ministerial Statement has 
instructed officials to continue working on outstanding issues with a renewed 
sense of urgency and purpose and taking fully into account all the views 
expressed in the Ministerial Conference. The Chairman of the General 
Council of the WHO, working in close coordination with the Director General,
